one_line: Paul Klein (Browserbase) argues reliable browser agents are a harness, tooling and infrastructure problem rather than a model problem, and lays out a multimodal, harness-engineered, consistently hosted approach.
summary: Klein says computer-use and browser agents lag behind coding agents even though models have improved, and he argues the gap is a "capabilities overhang" that engineering can close. He defines a harness as the scaffolding around a model (tools, memory, skills, sub-agents) and cites a same-model comparison where a domain-tuned harness beat a generic one. He says working browser agents are multimodal: they mix a vision model with code that replays network calls, so repeatable tasks become scripts. He covers harness tactics such as per-site skills, token-compact page representations and consistent infrastructure. He then argues the web itself needs to become agent-first through accessibility trees, WebMCP, agent-facing docs, agent sign-up and login flows, and some form of agent identity or trust. The talk closes with observability (recordings, logs, network traces) fed back into self-improvement, followed by a product pitch for Browserbase's new packaged agent harness.

key_ideas.idea: Browser agents are held back by the harness and tools, not the models
key_ideas.detail: He says models are now good at long-horizon and interface tasks, pointing to RL environments for computer use. He calls the remaining gap a capabilities overhang that engineering work (harness, tools, infra) should close.

key_ideas.idea: A harness tuned to the domain can beat the same model in a generic setup
key_ideas.detail: He cites a comparison where Factory's custom harness outperformed Claude Code on the same model. He says the harness should be measured against a baseline model, and that building one is an engineering task a non-lab team can do.

key_ideas.idea: Reliable browser agents combine a vision model with generated code
key_ideas.detail: Sometimes the agent should intercept network requests and write a script that replays them. Other times a stronger model handles a complex page and a cheaper one handles a simple page. Routing across models is part of the design.

key_ideas.idea: Per-site skills and memory make repeat tasks cheaper
key_ideas.detail: Browse.sh publishes skills for websites, so an agent can learn what a site supports before visiting it. Dumping the full page into the model gives worse results and costs more, so the harness should present a compressed, optimised set of tokens.

key_ideas.idea: Infrastructure consistency is a base layer
key_ideas.detail: Repeated runs should see the same layout, viewport and inputs. A page that renders mobile one time and desktop the next gives inconsistent results. Ad-hoc setups such as a home Mac mini cannot scale to thousands of agents or meet SOC 2.

key_ideas.idea: The web needs to become agent-first
key_ideas.detail: He points to accessibility trees and ARIA labels as better inputs than raw DOM, and to WebMCP as a way for sites to expose approved tool calls. He also mentions llms.txt, agents.md and skills.md as sites publishing agent-facing files.

key_ideas.idea: Authentication and trust are the next gate
key_ideas.detail: Sharing passwords or service accounts is risky. He suggests human-in-the-loop approval for sensitive actions and agent-first sign-up flows (WorkOS AuthMD). He describes web bot auth as a way for agents to identify themselves, and calls for a trusted certificate issuer for agents, a 'VeriSign moment'.
Each run should yield screen recordings, logs and network activity. That data loops back into the agent so it gets better every iteration. Browserbase's auto-browse does this across multiple loops.

techniques.name: Hybrid code-plus-browser execution
techniques.how: Use the browser to observe the page and capture network requests, then have the agent write and replay a script for those calls. Keep the vision model for pages that need it.
techniques.when: Repeatable web tasks in production, where a script is cheaper and more deterministic than click-by-click control.

techniques.name: Per-site skill packs loaded before visiting
techniques.how: Publish a skill describing a site's tasks and selectors. The agent reads it before navigating and updates it through memory after successful runs.
techniques.when: Agents that revisit the same websites often.

techniques.name: Compressed page representation
techniques.how: Pass accessibility-tree and ARIA subsections, not the full DOM or HTML, and include only the tokens needed for the next step.
techniques.when: Large or noisy pages where full-page context wastes tokens and lowers accuracy.

techniques.name: Pinned, consistent browser environment
techniques.how: Fix viewport, layout, locale and infrastructure across runs so each run sees the same inputs. Run on managed infrastructure rather than ad-hoc devices.
techniques.when: Any agent that runs the same flow many times or at scale.

techniques.name: Sites expose WebMCP tool calls and agent-first auth
techniques.how: Let the website publish tool calls (for example, submit registration) through WebMCP. Offer agent-specific sign-up and login, with human approval for sensitive actions.
techniques.when: Designing a site or service that agents will use, rather than only scraping it.

techniques.name: Observability-to-self-improvement loop
techniques.how: Store screen recordings, logs and network traces for each run, then feed them back to refine the agent's skills or harness over repeated loops.
techniques.when: Production browser agents where failures need diagnosing and success should compound over time.

numbers.claim: Vendor claim: Browserbase sees millions of sessions per month, which it uses to tune edge-case handling (no figures given beyond that)
Browserbase runs browser agents for thousands of customer agents in production (stated as a goal of the infrastructure, not a measured number)
Factory's custom harness outperformed Claude Code on the same model. A chart was shown but the numbers were not spoken.
Speaker cites Karpathy's harness framing tweet from November 2023 as an early prediction of the current design

hot_takes: Browser agent failures are an engineering and harness problem, not a model problem.
Teams should not wait for models to catch up; a company can build a good harness for its own domain.
Software now has to plan for agent users, with agent-first sign-up and login flows, whether or not the owner wants them.
A Mac mini setup cannot be made SOC 2 compliant at scale, so it is not a serious production answer for browser agents.
Agent trust needs a certificate-issuer model, similar to the TLS certificate authorities, and nobody has built it yet.

relevance.why: Speaker says a harness should bring skills and memory for repeat tasks, and that browser agents solve repeat tasks by writing code. AgentOS SkillForge mines telemetry into reusable skills, so a repeated web task is a candidate for that pipeline.
relevance.action: In SkillForge's open question on skill-worthiness, count a task as a candidate when an agent falls back to writing a replay script for a repeat web task. Log the signal in telemetry first.

relevance.why: Speaker names web bot auth (signed agent identity) and asks for a trust issuer for agents. The Govrix L1 proxy is the natural place to sign or identify agent traffic.
relevance.action: Read the web bot auth proposal and check whether Govrix could attach a signed agent identity to outbound agent requests.

relevance.why: Speaker says sites are starting to publish agent-facing files (llms.txt, agents.md, skills.md) and WebMCP tool manifests. A registry could index these as discovery sources for skills and MCP servers.
relevance.action: Read a few sites' llms.txt and WebMCP manifests and check whether the registry's discovery step can ingest them as a source.

relevance.why: Speaker's core claim is that a harness (tools, memory, skills, compact context) improves a model, and that it should be measured against the bare model. ProsHarness wraps Claude Code in exactly that kind of harness.
relevance.action: Run one repeated Claude Code task with and without ProsHarness and compare success rate and token use against the baseline, as the speaker advises.
